paras: The lynching of Ed Lewis and Kid George was the hanging of two Black men by a mob at Hattiesburg, Mississippi, on the night of August 4, 1905. Both were jailed as accomplices in the killing that morning of J. G. Smith, a white guard over the city convicts, and the mob took them from the jail and hanged them from a bridge. White papers called it an 'orderly' lynching, while a Hattiesburg mass meeting condemned it as 'cowardly murder'.

According to the first dispatches, a convict named Will Horn snatched Smith's pistol and shot him through the stomach. A special to the Mobile Register instead said Smith was 'assassinated' by Horn and 'Kid' George together. The two went to the home of Ed Lewis, called a 'notorious negro divekeeper', who with two women was said to have cut their shackles. Horn escaped, and several hundred men searched the country and swamps for him.

George was caught that afternoon at the yellow-fever quarantine line, where a soldier's bullet cut off his ear. He and Lewis were jailed after Lewis had been 'severely whipped' to make him say where Horn had gone. About 9 o'clock that night a crowd put at no less than 1,000 men broke into the jail and dragged the two out after a struggle.

They were hanged from a bridge in the glare of an electric light, Lewis fighting and cursing the mob and George begging for his life. Some wanted to burn the men and started a fire, which others put out, and shots were fired into the hanging bodies before the mob dispersed.

A San Juan paper reported that neither the police nor the national guard made a single arrest. On August 7 a mass meeting at the Hattiesburg city hall adopted resolutions condemning the 'cowardly murder' of Lewis and Kid George and pledging to help the courts bring the participants to justice. A special term of the circuit court was later urged to investigate citizens alleged to have taken part, but no report of an inquest, indictment or trial was found.

Horn was captured on August 17 by Sheriff Moody as a mob formed at Hattiesburg to lynch him. Governor Vardaman sent forty soldiers, who took Horn through Hattiesburg to the Jackson jail without an attempt on him. There Horn was reported to have confessed, implicated four other prisoners, and said that one of the lynched men was innocent.

The first wire report, from Mobile on August 4, said only that two Black men had killed a white man and 'a mob is after them'. The next day the Montgomery Advertiser headlined that the men 'Pay Penalty in Full Glare of the Electric Lights', and the Washington Evening Star headed its account 'An Orderly Lynching' although its text called the plot only 'alleged'. A two-line Memphis brief naming the men as 'accessories' then ran from South Carolina and Arkansas to Kentucky and Washington state. Later the St. Louis Republic took the militia's rescue of Horn as proof that Southern lynchers were 'not always implacably thirsty for African gore', and the Plymouth Tribune headlined Horn's claim 'Innocent Men Were Lynched'.

In the Black press the Cleveland Gazette carried only the Memphis brief. The Oklahoma Safeguard called the case Hattiesburg's 'fifth victim for Judge Lynch', described the two men as 'worthless characters', and declared, 'We have never favored lynching nor do we now.' It reprinted the mass-meeting resolutions, praised 'the good white people of Hattiesburg' for them, and quoted the Hattiesburg Weekly Times that no city paper had condemned the lynching and two had called it an 'orderly mob'.

The earliest dispatches and the San Juan account name Horn alone as the shooter, while the Register special and the fuller dispatch name Horn and George together. An Indiana item put the lynching on the day after the shooting, against the dispatches and the Hattiesburg resolutions. Horn's claim that one lynched man was innocent came from the accused shooter and was not tested in any reported proceeding.

reader.title: Lynching of Ed Lewis and Kid George
bases: A mob took two Black prisoners from the Hattiesburg city jail and hanged them from a bridge after the killing of a white convict guard (A5, A9, A22).

A mob put at 1,000 men broke into the city jail and hanged Ed Lewis and Kid George, charged as accomplices in the killing of guard J. G. Smith (A5, A9); a Hattiesburg mass meeting called it 'cowardly murder' and pledged to help bring the participants to justice (A22).

The Mobile Register special (A5, A7), a separate fuller dispatch (A4, A9), the Memphis wire (A12, A18), a Mississippi private letter (A3) and the Hattiesburg Daily Progress reprinted in the Black press (A22) agree that a mob took the two men from the jail and hanged them.

accounts.label: Mobile Register special
accounts.gist: Horn and Kid George 'assassinated' Smith; George was captured with Lewis, who had struck off the shackles; Lewis was whipped; at 9 o'clock a mob 'quietly' took both from jail and hanged them from a bridge.

accounts.label: Fuller press dispatch
accounts.gist: A mob of 1,000 broke into the jail after a struggle and hanged the two; some started a fire to burn them but others put it out; shots were fired into the bodies; the lynching was 'orderly'.

accounts.label: Hattiesburg mass meeting (Daily Progress)
accounts.gist: Local citizens condemned the 'cowardly murder' of Lewis and Kid George, taken out of the city jail on the night of Aug 4, and pledged to help bring the participants to justice.

accounts.label: Will Horn's statement
accounts.gist: After his capture Horn admitted the killing but said he never intended to kill and that one of the lynched men was innocent.

framing.detail: The Washington Evening Star headlined 'An Orderly Lynching' with the subhead 'A Mississippi Mob Dispatched Two Negro Murderers', and the Register special called the guard's death an assassination.
The Montgomery Advertiser headlined 'Two Blacks Lynched' and said the men 'Pay Penalty in Full Glare of the Electric Lights'.
Most papers ran a two-line Memphis brief naming the men as 'accessories' to the guard's murder, without comment.

The Plymouth Tribune headlined Horn's claim 'Innocent Men Were Lynched', and the St. Louis Republic took the militia's rescue of Horn as proof that Southern lynchers were 'not always implacably thirsty for African gore'.
The Cleveland Gazette ran only the Memphis wire brief, three times, under 'Two Negroes are Lynched'.
The Oklahoma Safeguard's 'Judge Lynch' item opposed the lynching while calling the victims worthless, reprinted the Hattiesburg resolutions, and quoted the Weekly Times on the 'orderly mob' phrase.
